title: Data, features & labels
intro: Rows are samples, columns are features, and the target is the column you predict — plus why the train/test split is non-negotiable.
keyPoints: Rows = samples, columns = features; the target column is y, the rest is X.
Numeric features go straight into the model; categorical features need encoding first (e.g. one-hot).
In scikit-learn, X is a 2D array (n × features) and y is a 1D array.
The train/test split is sacred: only evaluate on data the model has never seen.

sections.title: Thinking in tables: rows and columns

blocks.html: Every dataset is a table: rows are samples (one car, one e-mail), columns are variables. ML = finding patterns between columns.
Example: five cars, three features, price as target — kept small on purpose.
Jargon: feature = input column; target/label = the column you predict (mathematically: x and y).

sections.title: X and y: the scikit-learn convention

blocks.html: scikit-learn expects X (2D feature matrix, capital) and y (1D target vector, lowercase). Row i of X pairs with element i of y.

blocks.label: shape of the data
blocks.caption: n = number of samples (rows), p = number of features (columns). The model learns the mapping from each row x_i to a prediction y-hat.

blocks.html: This is how you turn the table into X and y with numpy — checking shapes is always your first step.

blocks.caption: the car table as X and y
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# rows = cars, columns = [age, mileage, owners]
X = np.array([[1,  5, 1],
              [3, 12, 2],
              [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3],
              [9, 30, 2]], dtype=float)

y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4])   # price (x1000 EUR)

print('X has shape:', X.shape, '-> n = 5 samples, p = 3 features')
print('y has shape:', y.shape, '-> 1 target per sample')
print('features of car 1:', X[0], '-> price:', y[0])

sections.title: Kinds of features (and how to prepare them)

blocks.html: Numeric = numbers. Categorical = labels: nominal (red/blue, no order) or ordinal (low/mid/high). Categoricals must be encoded: one-hot for nominal, 0/1/2 is fine for ordinal.

rows: larger scales dominate distance-based models → scale/standardise
one-hot encoding; never 1/2/3 — that suggests an order that is not there
may be 0/1/2, because the order is meaningful

blocks.html: Garbage in, garbage out: missing values, outliers and wrong encodings ruin any model. Exploring and cleaning data is often most of the work.

sections.title: Train and test: evaluate on unseen data

blocks.html: Golden rule: never evaluate on the data you train on. Hold out 75–80% for training and keep the rest as an honest test — you have not seen the real exam yet.
The mini-flow: split, train, print both scores. The train score is almost always higher; the test score is what counts.

blocks.caption: train/test split with KNN
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1], [3, 12, 2], [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3], [9, 30, 2], [2,  9, 1],
              [6, 20, 3], [8, 26, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4, 15, 8, 5], dtype=float)

# 75% train, 25% test — the model NEVER sees the test rows
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3).fit(X_train, y_train)
print('train score (optimistic):', model.score(X_train, y_train).round(2))
print('test score  (honest)    :', model.score(X_test, y_test).round(2))

new_car = [[5, 17, 1]]
print('predicted price (x1000 EUR):', model.predict(new_car)[0].round(1))

blocks.html: Train score is an optimistic diagnosis, test score the honest one. Only the test score says something about new data.
